sentences.text: Undisputedly, in the present case, the conviction is based solely on the dying declaration (Ext. Ka-6).
The law with regard to conviction on the sole basis of dying declaration has been considered by this Court in a catena of judgments.

After considering the earlier judgments, this Court, in the case of Atbir v. Government of NCT of Delhi, has laid down certain factors to be taken into consideration while resting the conviction on the basis of dying declaration.

It will be apposite to refer to para (22) of the said judgment, which reads thus:
"22.

The analysis of the above decisions clearly shows that:
(i) Dying declaration can be the sole basis of conviction if it Inspires the full confidence of the court.

sentences.text: (ii) The court should be satisfied that the deceased was in a fit state of mind at the time of making the statement and that it was not the result of tutoring, prompting or imagination.
https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis (iii) Where the court is satisfied that the declaration is true and voluntary, It can base its conviction without any further corroboration.
(iv) It cannot be laid down as an absolute rule of law that the dying declaration cannot form the sole basis of conviction unless it is corroborated.
The rule requiring corroboration is merely a rule of prudence.
(v.) Where the dying declaration is suspicious, it should not be acted upon without corroborative evidence.
(vi) A dying declaration which suffers from infirmity such as the deceased was unconscious and could never make any statement cannot form the basis of conviction.

(vii) Merely because a dying declaration does not contain all the details as to the occurrence, it is not to be rejected.
(viii) Even if it is a brief statement, it is not to be discarded.
(ix) When the eyewitness affirms that the deceased was not in a fit and conscious state to make the dying declaration, medical opinion cannot prevall.

(x) If after careful scrutiny, the court is https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis satisfied that it is true and free from any effort to induce the deceased to make a false statement and if it is coherent and consistent, there shall be no legal impediment to make it the basis of conviction, even if there is no corroboration 14.
It can thus be seen that this Court has clearly held that dying declaration can be the sole basis of conviction.
If it inspires the full confidence of the court.
The Court is required to satisfy itself that the deceased was in a fit state of mind at the time of making the statement and that it was not the result of tutoring, prompting or imagination.
It has further been held that, where the court is satisfied about the dying declaration being true and voluntary, it can be its conviction without any corroboration.
It further been held that there cannot be an absolute rule of law that the dying declaration cannot form the sole basis of condition unless it is cooperated.
It has been held that the rule requiring corroboration is merely a rule of oodles.

This court has observed that after careful scrutiny, satisfied that it is true and free from any effort induced the deceased to make a false statement and if it is coherent and consistent, there shall be no legal impediment to make it the basis of conviction, even if there is no corroboration.

The argument of the appellant counsel that when the Judicial Officer visited the Government Hospital, the victim was surrounded by four persons and Inspector of Police tutored the victim could not be acceptable as the victim in her complaint statement, and when she was admitted in the hospital repeatedly stated that the accused alone poured kerosene and set fire on her.

29. The learned Judicial Magistrate in her dying declaration clearly obtained certificate from the Doctor about the fitness of the victim and clearly had written in the certificate that except herself and the duty doctor, nobody was available near the victim when she had recorded her dying declaration.
Therefore, the argument advanced by the appellant counsel is not acceptable and we reject the same.
30. We are satisfied that the deceased was in a fit state of mind at the time of making the dying declaration and it was not the result of tutoring by anybody.
It was declared voluntarily and no corroboration is required, as she clearly stated, at the time of occurrence, nobody was available in the residence, except herself and the accused.

Soon after the occurrence, P.W.2, came to the house of the residence and found the https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis deceased with burn injuries admitted her into the hospital, which was supported by the evidence of P.W.10 who was treated her.
The evidence of victim inspires the confidence of Court.
Her evidence is consistent true and voluntary.
There is no reason to suspect her statement.

31. Further Section 32 of Indian Evidence Act deals with the Statements, written or verbal, or relevant facts, made by a person who is dead, or who cannot be found, or who has become incapable of giving evidence, or whose attendance cannot be procured, without an amount of delay or expense which under the circumstances of the case appears to the Court unreasonable, are themselves relevant facts in the following cases :
(1) When it relates to cause of death. - When the statement is made by a person as to the cause of his death, or as to any of the circumstances of the transaction which resulted in his death, in cases in which the cause of that person's death comes into question.

Such statements are relevant whether the person who made them was or was not, at the time when they were made, under https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis expectation of death, and whatever may be the nature of the proceeding in which the cause of his death comes into question.

32. Section 32 as a whole enunciates the exception to the rule of non-admissibility of hearsay evidence, emanated out of necessity to give relevant to the statements made by a person whose attendance cannot be procured for the reasons stipulate in the section.

Once a Dying Declaration is held to be authentic, inspiring full confidence beyond the pale of doubt, voluntary, consistent and credible, barren of tutoring, significant sanctity is endowed to it; such is the sanctitude that it can even be the exclusive and the solitary basis for conviction without seeking any corroboration.
(Ramakrishna Mishra vs. State of UP reported in 2015 (8) SCC 299.)

It is consistent and inspires the confidence of this Court and the conviction on the sole basis of dying declaration is proper and sustainable.

8. After full trial, the trial Court acquitted A2 to A5 from the charges and convicted the appellant/
accused No.1, for the offence punishable under Section 302 IPC and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life and to pay a sum of Rs.1,000/- in default, to undergo three months simple imprisonment, against which, the present Criminal Appeal is filed on the following among other grounds:-
(i) That the deceased sustained 95% burn injuries and hence, she is not capable of giving dying declaration.
https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis (ii) That the trial Court convicted the appellant on the basis of the circumstantial witness, there is no eye witness deposed against the appellant before the trial Court.
The Judicial Magistrate certified that she had ascertained the fit state of mind of the victim from the doctor and she also put some questions to the patient, and after having satisfied with the answer given by the patient recorded the statement.
. Further the Judicial Magistrate certified that the dying declaration was read over to the patient and obtained her left thumb impression.
opennyai_summary.issue: Now this court has to decide whether the judgement rendered by trial Court is proper or liable to be set aside.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Based on the complaint, FIR was registered in crime No.209/2013 for the offences under Sections 498A, 307 IPC based on the first information report,
the criminal law set into into motion.
In the complaint statement, she clearly pointed out that that her husband poured kerosene on her and set her ablaze and fled away from the place of occurrence.
The rule requiring corroboration is merely a rule of prudence.
(v.) Where the dying declaration is suspicious, it should not be acted upon without corroborative evidence.
(vi) A dying declaration which suffers from infirmity such as the deceased was unconscious and could never make any statement cannot form the basis of conviction.
It can thus be seen that this Court has clearly held that dying declaration can be the sole basis of conviction.
The Court is required to satisfy itself that the deceased was in a fit state of mind at the time of making the statement and that it was not the result of tutoring, prompting or imagination.
It was declared voluntarily and no corroboration is required, as she clearly stated, at the time of occurrence, nobody was available in the residence, except herself and the accused.
The evidence of victim inspires the confidence of Court.
Her evidence is consistent true and voluntary.
There is no reason to suspect her statement.
32. Section 32 as a whole enunciates the exception to the rule of non-admissibility of hearsay evidence, emanated out of necessity to give relevant to the statements made by a person whose attendance cannot be procured for the reasons stipulate in the section.
Once a Dying Declaration is held to be authentic, inspiring full confidence beyond the pale of doubt, voluntary, consistent and credible, barren of tutoring, significant sanctity is endowed to it; such is the sanctitude that it can even be the exclusive and the solitary basis for conviction without seeking any corroboration.
(Ramakrishna Mishra vs. State of UP reported in 2015 (8) SCC 299.)
Further Rule is that A person who is about to die would not lie Truth sits on the lips of a person w h o i s a b o u t t o d i e T h e l e g a l m a x i m n e m o m o r i t u r u s p r a e s u m i t u r m e n t i r e
It's also the term used to describe a dying declaration, which is a statement made by someone who is deceased.
35. We, therefore are of the opinion that dying declaration by the victim Ayyammal was made while she was expecting death and made in a fit state of mind, not tutored by anybody.
It is consistent and inspires the confidence of this Court and the conviction on the sole basis of dying declaration is proper and sustainable.
